subject: Medicine
summary: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic immune‑mediated disease causing demyelination and axonal loss in the CNS. It presents with relapsing neurological deficits and progressive disability.

sections.p: MS is defined by dissemination of lesions in space and time on MRI or clinically, plus exclusion of mimics. The 2017 McDonald criteria are used.
b: MRI brain/spine showing ≥2 T2 lesions in typical locations
CSF oligoclonal bands when MRI is equivocal

t.b: Does the patient have lesions in typical MS locations and at least two separate episodes? Positive lesions confirm dissemination in space and time.
Are oligoclonal IgG bands present? Their presence supports MS when MRI is nondiagnostic.
Is there delayed conduction in visual or somatosensory pathways? Helps demonstrate subclinical dissemination.

sections.p: Disability is measured with the Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS). Disease course is classified as relapsing‑remitting, secondary progressive, or primary progressive.
b: EDSS 0–3.5: mild, ambulatory without aid
EDSS ≥6.0: requires unilateral walking aid

sections.p: MS is autoimmune; genetic susceptibility (HLA‑DRB1*15:01) and environmental triggers (low vitamin D, EBV infection) are key.
b: Autoimmune demyelination (most common)
EBV infection as a possible trigger
Vitamin D deficiency, especially in higher latitudes

sections.p: Patients have episodes of optic neuritis, sensory loss, limb weakness, ataxia, or bladder dysfunction that remit partially.
b: Unilateral visual loss with pain on eye movement
Numbness or tingling spreading over hours
Limb weakness that improves over weeks

sections.p: MRI is the cornerstone; CSF and evoked potentials aid when MRI is unavailable or unclear.
b: MRI may be limited in low‑resource settings; consider referral or use of portable low‑field scanners.

t.b: Does imaging show typical periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal lesions? Positive findings confirm dissemination.
Are IgG bands present without serum counterparts? Supports diagnosis when MRI is equivocal.
Is P100 latency prolonged? Indicates demyelination of optic pathways.

sections.p: Acute severe relapse can cause optic neuritis with vision loss, spinal cord compression, or respiratory muscle weakness needing urgent care.
b: Sudden worsening of vision or breathing
New severe weakness or sphincter loss

sections.p: First‑line disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) reduces relapse frequency; acute relapses are treated with high‑dose IV methylprednisolone. Symptomatic care includes spasticity and bladder management.
b: Interferon‑β or glatiramer acetate: reduce immune activation, chosen for safety profile
Oral dimethyl fumarate: convenient, avoid if severe lymphopenia
Avoid natalizumab in JC‑virus positive patients due to PML risk

sections.p: Regular EDSS assessment every 6–12 months, MRI annually, and vitamin D supplementation. Counsel on smoking cessation and infection prevention.
b: Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus; avoid live vaccines during high‑dose steroids

sections.p: Conditions that mimic MS lesions or relapses.
b: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4‑IgG positive)
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (post‑infectious)
Sarcoidosis with CNS involvement

sections.p: Normal MRI early in disease or transiently negative CSF oligoclonal bands can give false reassurance.
b: Early MRI may miss spinal lesions; repeat imaging if clinical suspicion persists
Oligoclonal bands can be absent in up to 5 % of definite MS

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of vision in one eye
Rapidly worsening weakness or difficulty breathing

faq.a: No cure exists; treatment aims to reduce relapses and slow disability.
Hormonal and genetic factors increase susceptibility, especially during reproductive years.
No, it is an autoimmune disease, not an infection.

exam: List the 2017 McDonald criteria for diagnosing MS.
Explain how the EDSS is used to stage disease severity.
Describe first‑line disease‑modifying therapies and why natalizumab may be avoided.
related: JC virus and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
